lessons.topic: Verbs with an accusative object (Verben mit Akkusativobjekt)
lessons.title: The accusative
lessons.summary: The thing you order, buy, eat or have is in the accusative. Only der changes — to den.

cards.title: When do you need it?
cards.body: Ordering in a café, shopping, saying what you like: **Ich möchte einen Kaffee.** The person who does something is the subject (nominative); the thing you act on is the **object**, in the **accusative**.

examples.english: We need a table for two.

cards.title: Only masculine changes
cards.body: Good news: **die**, **das** and the plural stay the same. Only masculine **der → den**, **ein → einen**, **kein → keinen**.
cards.tip: der → den, ein → einen: the n is the accusative's signature.

cards.title: Verbs that take the accusative
cards.body: Most verbs with an object: **haben, möchten, nehmen, essen, trinken, kaufen, brauchen, mögen, bestellen, suchen, sehen**. Also **es gibt** (there is).

cards.title: sein is different
cards.body: After **sein** (and heißen, werden) there is **no** accusative: both sides are nominative.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Don't change feminine or neuter: **eine** Cola, **ein** Wasser — not 'einen Wasser'. And remember the n with masculine: **einen** Tee, **keinen** Zucker.

examples.german: Ich möchte **einen** Tee und **ein** Wasser, bitte.
examples.english: I'd like a tea and a water, please.

games.prompt: Ich möchte … : einen, eine or ein?
games.explanation: Only masculine changes: einen. Feminine eine, neuter ein.
der Kuchen → der Apfelkuchen is masculine: einen.

lessons.title: No article
lessons.summary: Sometimes German uses no article at all: for food in general, professions, countries and things you can't count.

cards.title: When do you need it?
cards.body: Saying what you like to eat or drink, your job, where you come from: **Ich trinke gern Tee.** **Ich bin Lehrerin.** **Ich komme aus Spanien.** No der/die/das, no ein.

cards.title: Food in general
cards.body: Uncountable food and drinks in general have no article: **Wasser, Milch, Brot, Käse, Reis, Zucker**. Countable things in general use the **plural** without article: **Äpfel, Eier, Kartoffeln**.

examples.english: Are you buying milk and eggs?
I like fish, but not cheese.

cards.tip: The negative of 'no article' is kein: Ich esse kein Fleisch.

cards.title: Jobs, nationalities, countries
cards.body: After **sein** and **werden** professions and nationalities have no article (unlike English 'a'). Most countries and all cities have no article either.

cards.title: But: some countries have one
cards.body: A few countries have an article: **die Schweiz, die Türkei, der Iran, die USA** (plural). Then you say **aus der Schweiz, in der Türkei**.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: Not 'Ich bin ein Lehrer' (unless you add an adjective). Not 'Ich trinke den Kaffee gern' when you mean coffee in general: **Ich trinke gern Kaffee**.

games.explanation: Jobs, food in general and most countries: no article. Die Schweiz, die Türkei have one.

games.prompt: Was bist du von Beruf? – Ich bin ___.
games.english: What's your job? – I'm a nurse.
games.explanation: Professions after sein have no article.
No article for food in general and jobs; negative with kein.

lessons.title: Punctuation
lessons.summary: Full stop, question mark, exclamation mark and the comma: the rules you need for messages, orders and e-mails.

cards.title: When does it matter?
cards.body: When you write a message, an order or a short e-mail. German punctuation is close to English, with a few differences — especially the **comma**.

cards.title: End of the sentence
cards.body: **.** for statements, **?** for every question (also polite ones), **!** for commands, strong feelings and often greetings in letters.

cards.title: The comma
cards.body: Use a comma in **lists** (but not before **und** / **oder**) and before **aber**, **sondern** and **denn**. In addresses: **Liebe Anna,** — then the next line starts with a **small** letter.

examples.english: I'd like bread, cheese and wine.

examples.german: Ich mag Tee**,** aber keinen Kaffee.
examples.english: I like tea, but not coffee.

cards.tip: No comma before und — the opposite of the Oxford comma.

cards.title: Capital letters
cards.body: Not punctuation, but just as important: **every noun** starts with a capital letter, and so does polite **Sie**. Days and languages used as nouns too: **am Montag**, **auf Deutsch**.

cards.title: Common mistakes
cards.body: No comma before **und** in a list. No capital letter after the comma in **Liebe Anna,**. And always a **?** after a question, even when it's a polite request.

examples.german:
Liebe Anna,
vielen Dank für die Einladung!
examples.english: Dear Anna, thank you for the invitation!

options: Ich trinke Tee, Saft, und Wasser.
Ich trinke Tee, Saft und Wasser.
Ich trinke Tee Saft und Wasser.
answers: Ich trinke Tee, Saft und Wasser.
games.explanation: Commas in a list, but none before und.

options: Ich esse gern Pizza aber keine Pasta.
Ich esse gern Pizza und Pasta.
answers: Ich esse gern Pizza aber keine Pasta.
games.explanation: aber needs a comma before it: …Pizza, aber keine Pasta.
